workflow.title: Cancellation Policy: Short-Notice Cancellations and Charging
workflow.description: How to handle a client cancellation with less than 48 hours' notice: why it matters, the steps to work through, how the reminder and travel shape what can be charged, and what you must discuss with your supervisor before any charge is decided. Three interactive walkthroughs, a practical task and a knowledge check.

items.title: Walkthrough: Why short-notice cancellations matter
items.body:
How a late cancellation affects clients, your day and the practice, the 48-hour starting point, and where the rules sit.

Your progress is saved if you stop part-way.

items.title: Walkthrough: Handling a short-notice cancellation
items.body: The four steps to work through when a client cancels with less than 48 hours' notice, including how to consider the reason, with decision checks along the way.

items.title: Reference: step by step
items.body:
When a client cancels with less than 48 hours' notice:

- **Try to fill the time** with other work first. We always do this.
- If you cannot fill it, **talk to your supervisor** about how it affects your billable hours for the week.
- **Consider the reason** for the cancellation and whether it was beyond the client's control.
- **Check the facts** on reminders and travel.

Do not push clients for private details they do not want to share.

**Discuss with your supervisor before deciding whether to charge.**

items.title: Walkthrough: Reminders, travel and charging
items.body: How the reminder and whether travel had started shape what can be charged, followed by two scenarios with made-up clients.

items.title: Reference: reminder and travel
items.body:
Two facts shape what can be charged.

- **Travel had started, a reminder was sent and the client did not respond:** the full time you had blocked, plus travel time.
- **Travel had not started:** the session time, but not travel time.
- **Exception:** if the cancellation affects other clients' travel, travel time may still come into the discussion. Raise it with your supervisor.
- **Clients bunched in a similar location:** the same rules apply.

The rules sit in the client's service agreement and in the NDIS pricing guideline. Always read the actual service agreement for the client in front of you, and discuss with your supervisor before deciding whether to charge.

items.title: Practical task: walk through a cancellation
items.body:
Pick a past or made-up cancellation with less than 48 hours' notice. Write down your answers to these checks:

- Could the time be filled with other work?
- Was a reminder sent, and did the client respond?
- Had travel started?
- Was other clients' travel affected?
- Was the reason beyond the client's control?

Then go through your answers with your supervisor.

items.title: Knowledge check
items.body: Eight questions across the whole induction. You need 80% to pass, and you may retry.

questions.question: A client cancels with less than 48 hours' notice. What do you do first?
options: Charge the full amount straight away
Try to fill the time with other work
Ask the client to explain the reason in detail
Leave it until the end of the week

questions.question: You cannot fill the cancelled time. What do you do next?
options: Talk to your supervisor about the effect on your weekly billable hours
Cancel the client's service agreement
Charge the client without discussing it
Say nothing and move on

questions.question: A reminder was sent, the client did not respond, and you had started travelling when the session was cancelled. If a charge goes ahead, what is the approach?
options: No charge at all
Session time only
The full blocked time plus travel time
Travel time only

questions.question: You had not started travelling when the client cancelled, and no other clients are affected. What can be charged?
options: Session time, but not travel time
Travel time, but not session time
Nothing, in any circumstances
Both session time and travel time

questions.question: You had not started travelling, but the cancellation affects another client's travel. What should you do?
options: Treat it exactly the same as any other cancellation
Raise it with your supervisor, as travel may be part of the discussion
Cancel the other client too
Charge travel time without discussing it

questions.question: Which is true of the reason for a short-notice cancellation?
options: The reason never matters
You must ask the client for full personal details
Consider whether it was beyond the client's control, and discuss it with your supervisor
Only the client decides whether a charge applies

questions.question: You had several clients bunched in a similar location. Which rules apply to a short-notice cancellation?
options: No charge can apply to bunched clients
The same rules apply
Travel time is always charged to every client
Only the first client's rules apply

questions.question: Where do the rules on short-notice cancellations sit?
options: In the client's service agreement and the NDIS pricing guideline
Only in your calendar
In a verbal agreement with the client
In the therapist's own notes

items.title: Cancellation policy sign-off
items.body: Confirm that you understand how short-notice cancellations are handled at Opal.
items.ack_statement: I have read this induction. I understand that a cancellation with less than 48 hours' notice can be charged under the service agreement, and that this is a starting point only. I will try to fill the time first, check the reminder, travel and the reason, read the client's actual service agreement, and discuss with my supervisor before deciding whether to charge.

walkthroughs.title: Why short-notice cancellations matter
walkthroughs.description: How a late cancellation affects clients, your day and the practice, the 48-hour starting point, and where the rules sit.

steps.title: Why this matters

image.alt: On a rural run, one short-notice cancellation affects the whole run of visits.

steps.body:
Late cancellations affect clients, your day and Opal's ability to keep running.

When a session is cancelled at short notice, you may lose billable time and travel that cannot be recovered. In rural and remote areas, **one cancellation can affect a whole run of visits**.

steps.title: Fair to clients and to Opal
steps.body:
Charging is not a simple switch. We look at:
• **what** happened
• **why** it happened
• **who** was affected

Our aim is to be fair to clients and to Opal.

steps.title: The 48-hour starting point

image.alt: A cancellation with less than 48 hours' notice can be charged under the service agreement; this is a starting point only.

steps.body:
Under our service agreement, a cancellation with **less than 48 hours' notice can be charged**.

This is a starting point only. First try to fill the time, then check the circumstances, and then talk to your supervisor.

quiz.question: A client cancels 30 hours before a session. Which statement is correct?
options: The client decides whether a charge applies
A charge can be considered under the service agreement, but this is a starting point only
No charge can apply, whatever the circumstances
quiz.explain: Less than 48 hours' notice can be charged under the service agreement, but this is a starting point only. First try to fill the time, then check the circumstances and talk to your supervisor.

steps.title: Where the rules sit

image.alt: The client's service agreement and the NDIS pricing guideline.

steps.body:
The rules sit in the client's **service agreement** and in the **NDIS pricing guideline**.

Always read the actual service agreement for the client in front of you.

quiz.question: A client has cancelled at short notice and you are preparing to talk to your supervisor. Which service agreement do you read?
options: A general template agreement
The actual service agreement for that client
The agreement of a similar client
quiz.explain: The rules sit in the client's own service agreement, so always read the actual agreement for the client in front of you.

steps.title: Summary: why short-notice cancellations matter
steps.body:
Less than 48 hours' notice can be charged under the service agreement, but this is a starting point only, and the client's own service agreement is the one to read.

Return to your induction to continue with the next module: handling a short-notice cancellation.

walkthroughs.title: Handling a short-notice cancellation
walkthroughs.description: The four steps to work through when a client cancels with less than 48 hours' notice, and how to consider the reason.

steps.title: The four steps

image.alt: Fill the time, talk to your supervisor, consider the reason, check reminder and travel.

steps.body:
When a client cancels with less than 48 hours' notice, work through these steps:
• **Try to fill the time** with other work first. We always do this.
• If you cannot fill it, **talk to your supervisor** about how it affects your billable hours for the week.
• **Consider the reason** for the cancellation and whether it was beyond the client's control.
• **Check the facts** on reminders and travel.

Discuss with your supervisor before deciding whether to charge.

quiz.question: A client cancels with less than 48 hours' notice. What do you do first?
options: Charge the client straight away
Try to fill the time with other work
Ask the client to explain the reason in detail
quiz.explain: We always try to fill the cancelled time with other work first.

steps.title: Knowledge check: when the time cannot be filled

quiz.question: You have tried, but you cannot fill the cancelled time. What do you do next?
options: Talk to your supervisor about the effect on your weekly billable hours
Charge the client without discussing it
Leave the gap and say nothing
quiz.explain: If the time cannot be filled, talk to your supervisor about how it affects your billable hours for the week.

steps.title: Consider the reason
steps.body:
Always think about why the session was cancelled. Ask yourself: **was it beyond the client's control?**

A reason outside the client's control is something to raise with your supervisor before any charge is decided.

steps.title: Respect the client's privacy
steps.body: Do not push clients for private details they do not want to share.

steps.title: Scenario: a reason outside the client's control

quiz.question: A client cancels on the morning of a session, saying only that a family emergency has come up. You cannot fill the time. What do you do next?
options: Ask for full details of the emergency so you can decide on a charge
Consider whether it was beyond the client's control, and raise it with your supervisor before any charge is decided
Charge the client, as the notice was less than 48 hours
quiz.explain: A reason outside the client's control is raised with your supervisor before any charge is decided. Do not push the client for private details they do not want to share.

steps.title: Before deciding whether to charge
steps.body:
Discuss with your supervisor before deciding whether to charge.

The next module covers the facts that shape what can be charged: the reminder and travel.

steps.title: Summary: handling a short-notice cancellation
steps.body:
Fill the time first, talk to your supervisor if you cannot, consider the reason, check the reminder and travel facts, and discuss with your supervisor before deciding whether to charge.

Return to your induction to continue with the next module: reminders, travel and charging.

walkthroughs.title: Reminders, travel and charging
walkthroughs.description: How the reminder and whether travel had started shape what can be charged, with two scenarios using made-up clients.

steps.title: What decides the charge

image.alt: Travel started, reminder sent and no response: full blocked time plus travel time. Travel not started: session time, not travel time. Other clients' travel affected: raise it with your supervisor.

steps.body:
Two facts shape what can be charged.

**Travel had started, a reminder was sent and the client did not respond:** the full time you had blocked, plus travel time.

**Travel had not started:** the session time, but not travel time.

**Exception:** if the cancellation affects other clients' travel, travel time may still come into the discussion with your supervisor.

If you had clients bunched in a similar location, the same rules apply.

quiz.question: A reminder was sent, the client did not respond, and you had started travelling when the session was cancelled. If a charge goes ahead, what is the approach?
options: No charge at all
Session time only
The full blocked time plus travel time
Travel time only
quiz.explain: With a reminder sent, no response and travel started, the approach is the full blocked time plus travel time.

steps.title: Knowledge check: travel had not started

quiz.question: You had not started travelling when the client cancelled, and no other clients are affected. What can be charged?
options: Session time, but not travel time
Travel time, but not session time
Both session time and travel time
quiz.explain: Session time can be charged, but not travel time, because you had not travelled.

quiz.question: You had not started travelling, but the cancellation affects another client's travel. What should you do?
options: Treat it exactly the same as any other cancellation
Raise it with your supervisor, as travel may be part of the discussion
Cancel the other client's visit too
quiz.explain: The rule on travel time has an exception where other clients' travel is affected, and that is raised with your supervisor.

steps.title: Scenario: travel already started

image.alt: A reminder was sent, Sam did not reply, you were on the road, and Sam cancelled 20 hours before the session.

steps.body:
**Situation:** A reminder went to a made-up client, Sam. Sam did not reply. You left for the visit and were on the road when Sam cancelled, 20 hours before the session time.

Decide what you would do on the next two screens.

steps.title: Scenario: Sam cancels while you are on the road

quiz.question: Sam has just cancelled and you are on the road. What do you do first?
options: Charge Sam the full blocked time plus travel time
Try to fill the time with other work
Ask Sam to explain the reason in detail
quiz.explain: Whatever the circumstances, the first step is always to try to fill the time with other work.

steps.title: Scenario: Sam's time cannot be filled

quiz.question: You cannot fill the time. A reminder was sent, Sam did not reply and you had already started travelling. What do you do next?
options: Charge session time only, without discussing it
Talk to your supervisor about the effect on your week and consider Sam's reason; if a charge goes ahead, the approach is the full blocked time plus travel time
Charge travel time only
quiz.explain: Your supervisor is part of the decision. If a charge goes ahead with a reminder sent, no response and travel started, the approach is the full blocked time plus travel time.

steps.title: Scenario: travel not started

image.alt: Priya cancels the evening before and you have not left; Tom lives nearby and is booked after Priya.

steps.body:
**Situation:** A made-up client, Priya, cancels the evening before a morning session. You have not left yet. Another made-up client, Tom, lives nearby and was booked after Priya.

Decide what you would do on the next two screens.

steps.title: Scenario: Priya cancels the evening before

quiz.question: You have tried to fill the time. What do you check next, before talking to your supervisor?
options: Whether Priya's cancellation affects Tom's travel or other bunched visits
Whether Priya can provide evidence of the reason
Nothing, as travel time is always charged
quiz.explain: Check whether the cancellation affects Tom's travel or other bunched visits, then talk to your supervisor.

quiz.question: You find that Priya's cancellation affects Tom's travel. What do you do?
options: Charge Priya session time and travel time straight away
Raise it with your supervisor
Cancel Tom's visit as well
quiz.explain: If nothing else were affected, the session time could be charged but not travel time. Because Tom's travel is affected, raise it with your supervisor.

steps.title: Summary: reminders, travel and charging
steps.body:
If travel had started, a reminder was sent and the client did not respond, the approach is the full blocked time plus travel time; if travel had not started, it is session time only; and where other clients' travel is affected, raise it with your supervisor.

Return to your induction to complete the practical task, the knowledge check and the sign-off.

policy.name: Cancellation and Late Cancellation Charges
policy.summary: Cancellations with less than 48 hours' notice can be charged under the service agreement, depending on whether travel had started, whether a reminder was sent and the circumstances, with supervisor discussion first.
